plan.contextChunk: This figure is a labeled anatomy diagram of a horizontal ellipse, drawn as a blue outline centered at the origin of a coordinate system whose horizontal axis is marked x at the right and whose vertical axis is marked y at the top, both ending in arrowheads. A red dashed segment lies along the horizontal axis and spans the full width of the curve; the words "Major Axis" sit below its left half, and its two endpoints, where the outline meets the horizontal axis, are marked with dots and labeled "Vertex" at each end. A second red dashed segment lies along the vertical axis and spans the height of the curve, labeled "Minor Axis" beside its upper half, with black dots at its ends labeled "Co-vertex" above and "Co-vertex" below. The black dot where the two dashed segments cross is labeled "Center." Two small green dots sit on the horizontal dashed segment, one on either side of the center and well inside the vertices, each labeled "Focus." Collecting every named part on a single outline lets the reader tie each term to a definite position relative to the center. The diagram supplies the vocabulary needed to set up and read the standard equation of an ellipse.

interactionPlan.concept: The anatomical features of an ellipse—its vertices, co-vertices, and foci—are determined by the lengths of its major and minor axes, which correspond directly to the distance parameters a, b, and c.
elements: x-axis (horizontal) with right arrowhead and 'x' label
y-axis (vertical) with top arrowhead and 'y' label
blue elliptical curve centered at the origin
red dashed horizontal line segment spanning the ellipse width
red dashed vertical line segment spanning the ellipse height
black dot at the origin (Center)
two blue dots at the horizontal extremes (Vertices)
two black dots at the vertical extremes (Co-vertices)
two green dots on the longer axis (Foci)
Anatomy labels: 'Center', 'Vertex' (x2), 'Co-vertex' (x2), 'Focus' (x2), 'Major Axis', 'Minor Axis'
Parameter labels (visible only in parameter mode): dimension brackets or lines indicating distance 'a' (center to vertex), 'b' (center to co-vertex), and 'c' (center to focus)

interactions.label: Horizontal radius (a)
interactions.teaches: Stretching the horizontal dimension moves the vertices further out and forces the foci to shift outward to maintain the geometric definition of the ellipse.

interactions.label: Vertical radius (b)
interactions.teaches: Changing the vertical dimension alters the ellipse's height; if the vertical radius becomes larger than the horizontal radius, it takes over as the major axis.

interactions.label: Display mode
interactions.teaches: The descriptive vocabulary of an ellipse translates exactly into the distance variables used in its standard mathematical equation.

demo_steps.title: Ellipse Anatomy
demo_steps.narration: An ellipse has two axes of symmetry. The longer one is the Major Axis (ending at the Vertices), and the shorter is the Minor Axis (ending at the Co-vertices).

demo_steps.title: Stretching the Major Axis
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the horizontal radius stretches the ellipse. The vertices move outward, and the foci shift away from the center along with them.

demo_steps.title: Swapping Axes
demo_steps.narration: If you increase the vertical dimension until it exceeds the horizontal dimension, the ellipse becomes vertical. The vertical axis is now the Major Axis, and the foci snap to it.

demo_steps.title: Mapping Anatomy to Equations
demo_steps.narration: Switching to equation parameters reveals how vocabulary ties to math: 'a' is the distance to a vertex, 'b' to a co-vertex, and 'c' to a focus.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The foci always live on the major (longer) axis; if the minor axis is stretched to become the longer one, it structurally becomes the new major axis.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Render a standard coordinate plane with a prominent blue ellipse. Use dashed red segments inside the ellipse for the axes. Mark the center (black), vertices (blue), co-vertices (black), and foci (green). In Anatomy mode, place standard text labels near their respective dots. In Parameter mode, hide the anatomy words and instead show dimensional brackets from the center: 'a' out to a vertex, 'b' up to a co-vertex, and 'c' out to a focus. Ensure c is dynamically calculated as sqrt(|a^2 - b^2|) so the foci snap to the y-axis if b > a.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for semi-major axis a: the learner drags the horizontal radius, the vertices and major axis stretch while the center stays fixed, and a controls the ellipse's width.
- Slider for semi-minor axis b: the learner drags the vertical radius, the co-vertices and minor axis move while the horizontal vertices stay fixed, and b controls the ellipse's height.
- Toggle between feature labels and equation parameters: the learner switches from center, vertices, co-vertices, and foci labels to a, b, and c distances, showing how the named parts map onto the standard ellipse equation.

authoredContext:
Every ellipse has two axes of symmetry. The longer axis is called the major axis, and the shorter axis is called the minor axis. Each endpoint of the major axis is the vertex of the ellipse (plural: vertices), and each endpoint of the minor axis is a co-vertex of the ellipse. The center of an ellipse is the midpoint of both the major and minor axes. The axes are perpendicular at the center. The foci always lie on the major axis, and the sum of the distances from the foci to any point on the ellipse (the constant sum) is greater than the distance between the foci. See the figure.

A horizontal ellipse centered at (0, 0) in the x y coordinate system, with Major and Minor Axes, Vertices and Co-Vertices, Foci, and Center labeled.

In this section, we restrict ellipses to those that are positioned vertically or horizontally in the coordinate plane. That is, the axes will either lie on or be parallel to the x- and y-axes. Later in the chapter, we will see ellipses that are rotated in the coordinate plane.

discrepancies: The source figure has a plain white background, whereas the generated figure includes a full Cartesian grid
The axes in the source figure terminate exactly at the ellipse's bounds (vertices and co-vertices) with arrowheads, but the generated axes extend far beyond the ellipse
The ellipse in the generated figure has a faint blue fill, while the source ellipse is entirely unfilled/transparent
Text labels in the generated figure are colored to match their features (blue for Vertex, green for Focus, red for Major/Minor Axis), whereas all text in the source is black
The 'Major Axis' label is placed on the right half of the ellipse in the generated figure, rather than the left half as in the source
evaluation.notes: The interactive demo and equation parameter toggles provide excellent pedagogical value, but the generated figure deviates visually from the source by adding a grid, extending the axes beyond the ellipse, and coloring the text labels.
action_items: Remove the background grid lines to match the clean background of the source figure
Shorten the x and y axes so they terminate exactly at the vertices and co-vertices of the ellipse, matching the bounds in the source
Remove the faint blue fill from the ellipse so it is completely transparent
Change the fill color of all text labels (Vertex, Focus, Major Axis, Minor Axis) to black
Move the 'Major Axis' label to the left side of the y-axis to match the source placement
